sections.name: C++ for Games
sections.explanation_simple: C++ is like the engine of a race car - it's powerful, fast, and gives you total control. Most AAA games like Fortnite, Call of Duty, and Unreal Engine are written in C++. Think of it as the 'professional sports car' of programming languages - harder to drive than an automatic (like Python), but way faster when you know what you're doing.
key_concepts: Variables store data (int health = 100;)
Functions are reusable blocks of code
Classes are blueprints for objects
Pointers store memory addresses (& and *)
The game loop runs 60 times per second
Smart pointers prevent memory leaks
STL provides ready-made data structures
Move semantics transfer resources efficiently

sections.learning_path: Learn C basics first (variables, loops, functions) -> C++ classes and objects -> Pointers and memory -> STL containers -> Game loop implementation -> Build small games (Pong, Snake) -> Study ECS patterns -> Study game engine source code

sections.name: C# for Unity
sections.explanation_simple: C# is like C++'s younger cousin that's safer and easier to use. Unity uses C# for all game logic. If C++ is a manual sports car, C# is an automatic - you still get great performance but you don't have to worry about memory leaks as much. Unity handles all the hard graphics stuff, you just tell it what to do with C# scripts.
key_concepts: MonoBehaviour is the base class for all game scripts
Awake() runs once when object is created
Start() runs once before first Update
Update() runs every frame (60 times/second)
FixedUpdate() runs at fixed intervals (good for physics)
GameObject is everything in the scene
GetComponent<T>() gets components attached to an object
Instantiate() creates copies of objects
Coroutines let you spread code over time
Serialization shows variables in the Unity Inspector

sections.learning_path: Unity Learn tutorials -> C# basics (variables, if/else, loops) -> MonoBehaviour methods -> Simple 2D game -> 3D movement -> Physics -> UI -> Audio -> Build a complete game

sections.name: HLSL & Shader Programming
sections.explanation_simple: Shaders are tiny programs that run on your GPU (graphics card) to draw every single pixel on screen. While regular code runs on the CPU, shaders run THOUSANDS of times in parallel. Think of it like this: if normal programming is giving instructions to one chef, shader programming is giving instructions to 1000 chefs all cooking at once. That's why games can render millions of pixels 60 times per second.
key_concepts: Vertex shader transforms 3D positions to screen positions
Pixel/Fragment shader colors each pixel
HLSL is the shader language for DirectX (Xbox, PC)
GLSL is for OpenGL (cross-platform)
Metal Shading Language is for Apple devices
Compute shaders do general-purpose GPU work
Semantics like SV_POSITION connect shader stages
GPU runs thousands of threads in parallel (SIMT)

sections.learning_path: Learn how GPUs work -> Basic vertex/pixel shaders -> Lighting models (Phong, PBR) -> Post-processing effects -> Compute shaders -> Advanced techniques (tessellation, geometry shaders)

sections.name: Rust for Games
sections.explanation_simple: Rust is the new hotness in game development. It's like C++ but with a safety guarantee - the compiler prevents you from making memory mistakes (which cause 70% of serious game bugs). Think of Rust as C++'s strict but helpful older sibling who won't let you crash the car. Companies like Embark Studios are building AAA games in Rust right now.
key_concepts: Ownership - every value has exactly one owner
Borrowing - references without taking ownership (& and &mut)
Lifetimes - compiler tracks how long references are valid
No null pointers - Option<T> instead
No dangling pointers - ownership system prevents them
Traits are like interfaces in C++/Java
Pattern matching with match statements
Cargo is the build system and package manager
WASM compilation - run Rust games in browser
unsafe code for low-level control when needed

sections.learning_path: Learn Rust basics (variables, functions) -> Ownership and borrowing -> Structs and enums -> Traits and generics -> Error handling -> Bevy game engine -> WASM deployment

sections.name: Game Mathematics
sections.explanation_simple: Game math is the invisible language that makes everything work. When you press 'W' and your character walks forward, that's vector math. When you spin the camera around, that's matrix multiplication. When a grenade explodes and pushes enemies back, that's physics math. You don't need to be a math genius - you just need to understand a few key concepts and how to use them in code.
key_concepts: Vectors represent position, direction, velocity (3 floats: x, y, z)
Dot product tells you how aligned two directions are
Cross product gives a perpendicular direction
Matrices transform coordinates (translate, rotate, scale)
Quaternions rotate things without gimbal lock issues
Lerp (linear interpolation) smoothly transitions between values
Delta time makes movement framerate-independent
Easing curves make animations feel natural

sections.learning_path: 2D coordinates (x,y) -> Vector addition/subtraction -> Dot product -> Cross product -> 3D coordinates -> Matrices (rotate/scale/translate) -> Quaternions -> Matrix transforms for camera -> Physics integration

sections.name: Design Patterns for Games
sections.explanation_simple: Design patterns are like recipes for common problems in game programming. Instead of inventing solutions from scratch, you use patterns that generations of game programmers have figured out. They're not strict rules - just proven approaches to make your code cleaner, faster, and easier to change.
key_concepts: Singleton: One global instance (GameManager, AudioManager)
Observer: One object tells many others when something happens (event system)
State Machine: Objects can only be in one state at a time (Idle, Walking, Jumping, Attacking)
Command: Turn actions into objects (undo/redo, input binding)
Object Pool: Reuse objects instead of creating/destroying (bullets, particles)
Flyweight: Share data between many objects (tree instances sharing one mesh)
Factory: Create objects without specifying exact class
Component: Compose behavior by attaching components (Unity/Unreal way)

sections.learning_path: Singleton first (simplest) -> State Machine (most useful) -> Observer/Event Bus -> Object Pool -> Command Pattern -> Component Pattern -> Factory Pattern
